“Carl Th. Dreyer was a modest man, as were his sitting room and, later, his grave. Carl Th. Dreyer possessed the pure heart and natural humility of the passionate individual. Carl Th. Dreyer’s passion was FILM.” — Lars von Trier

Denmark’s first great filmmaker, Carl Theodor Dreyer worked between 1919 and 1964…. though sadly he only completed four features in the last 30 years of his life. Each of these films (Vampyr; Day of Wrath; Ordet; Gertrud) is considered a masterpiece, as is his silent film, The Passion of Joan of Arc. Many of his films (like Lars on Trier’s) focus on the persecution of women. In Dreyer’s case this is invariably in the service of social critique, contrasting female sexuality and power with the repressive strictures of the Church.

In Day of Wrath, Anna, the young second wife of a well-respected but much older pastor, falls in love with her stepson when he returns to their small seventeenth-century village. Stepping outside the bounds of the village’s harsh moral code has disastrous results. Exquisitely photographed and passionately acted, Day of Wrath remains an intense, unforgettable experience. Made during the Nazi Occupation of Denmark, it has been interpreted as an anti-fascist allegory.

Sunday’s Pantheon screening will feature a 15-minute introduction by a local film scholar and be followed by an audience talkback.

 

Mar 15: Intro by Kiran K. Sunar, Assistant Professor, Department of Asian Studies, UBC

Kiran’s research and teaching coagulate around literature, religion, and cinema in Punjab and its diasporas, exploring questions of gender, sexuality, religion, and ecology. Their scholarship often blends critical and creative modes.

 

Dreyer’s impious, anarchic drama is a cry of rage at abusive authority, whether political, familial, religious, or moral; he celebrates erotic love as the natural order of things.

Richard Brody, New Yorker

Astonishing in its artistically informed period re-creation as well as its hypnotic mise en scene, it challenges the viewer by suggesting at times that witchcraft isn’t so much an illusion as an activity produced by intolerance.

Jonathan Rosenbaum

A stark, brooding treatment of adultery, incest, and murder, an elemental tragedy not so far from a James M. Cain triangle, albeit shot so as to deliberately evoke the Dutch masters.

J Hoberman, Village Voice

Baghdad, 2003. The Khachaturian family take a wrong turn and wind up in the middle of a firefight. US Marines open fire on their car; there are multiple casualties. Ten years later, San Diego. Lou (Boyd Holbrook) still has nightmares about that day. He’s working as a bouncer and a construction worker, trying to get into law school, but his body is racked with guilt. He reaches out to an American journalist who reported on the deaths of the Khachaturians, Michael (Kenneth Branagh) and asks if he can broker a meeting with the survivors…

First time writer-director Reed Van Dyk gets a big assist from veteran Palestinian actress Hiam Abbass as the matriarch of the Iraqi family, and who becomes the film’s focal point in the simple, but very moving, last act.

title:
My Undesirable Friends: Part II — Exile

5:30 pm 365 min

Film

Julia Loktev's follow up to last year's film about dissident journalists in Moscow tracks the reporters as they are forced into exile across a four year period, but still striving to counterbalance state propaganda as Putin pursues the war in Ukraine.
Book Now More Info
moreInfo:
A group of young journalists flee Moscow when Russia invades Ukraine and shuts down all independent media, turning telling the truth into a crime. Just days before, they were working as part of a vibrant opposition community. Now they’re part of a historic exodus. They leave with a few hours’ notice, carry-on suitcases, and no idea what country they can go to next that will let them stay and keep working. They must quickly get back on their feet to report on the biggest story of their lives, a war they all fiercely oppose.

Intimate and immersive, the film sweeps across four years and a dozen countries. The complex, razor sharp and often very funny women — and a few men — gather in apartments that feel like waystations and borrowed offices before being uprooted yet again. They work to bring Russians an alternative to propaganda, speaking out against their country’s war crimes and wrestling with personal moral accountability, even as Russia menaces them with criminal prosecution back home and physical threats abroad. Relying on dark humor to get through dark times, they keep working for the uncertain future of a country they may not return to for decades. As the years pass in exile, they have to redefine what work, family, friendship, love and home mean when you can’t go home.

title:
Once Upon a Time in Harlem

1:30 pm 110 min

Film

Once Upon a Time in Harlem splices together footage shot by William Greaves in 1972 of a group of Harlem Renaissance luminaries in conversation at Duke Ellington’s townhouse. The film is a living archive of memory, disagreement, style, and Black genius.
Book Now More Info
moreInfo:
In 1972, pioneering filmmaker William Greaves gathered surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance inside Duke Ellington’s townhouse and let the cameras roll. Eubie Blake, James Van Der Zee, Arna Bontemps, Richard Bruce Nugent, Gerri Major, Romare Bearden, and others reminisce, argue, laugh, interrupt, and remember a movement built from Black genius in motion. More than 50 years later, Once Upon a Time in Harlem arrives as a moving-image artifact, alive with the presence of its towering figures returned right into the room.

Greaves, the visionary behind Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One (1968), left behind 60,000 feet of 16mm footage to be rediscovered for this film. His son David Greaves (one of the original camera operators) and David’s daughter Liani bring the footage into the present as both family inheritance and public archive. Premiering at Sundance before screening in Cannes Directors’ Fortnight, the film is a portal into a room of style, memory, disagreement, and brilliance that reminds us a renaissance is not only remembered, it is reborn.

It’s both a sublime hang-out of a film and a celebration of individual achievements, a fascinating map of a long-ago scene and a referendum on legacy. That this sumptuous footage, allowed room to breathe, exists at all feels like a miracle; that it takes shape here as a coherent, inventive yet straightforwardly informative film is an intergenerational feat… a faultless, captivating experience.

Adrian Horton, The Guardian

No matter one’s distance from the Harlem Renaissance, Once Upon A Time In Harlem transforms its cultural milieu into personal memory, suffusing history with enormity and reinvigorating it for generations to come.

Siddhant Adlakha, Observer

The conversations could not be more stimulating, offering a glimpse of Black America past and present that is joyous, defiant and sobering.

Tim Grierson, Screen International

Nor does he hang his scientist for Frankensteinian hubris. Rather, this is a film about fusion. The playful, quirky chemistry established between Goldblum and Davis (they married soon after) ensures that this gothic horror is heartbreaking as well as stomach churning, though the special effects by Chris Walas remain staggering even today. In 1972, pioneering filmmaker William Greaves gathered surviving luminaries of the Harlem Renaissance inside Duke Ellington’s townhouse and let the cameras roll. Eubie Blake, James Van Der Zee, Arna Bontemps, Richard Bruce Nugent, Gerri Major, Romare Bearden, and others reminisce, argue, laugh, interrupt, and remember a movement built from Black genius in motion. More than 50 years later, Once Upon a Time in Harlem arrives as a moving-image artifact, alive with the presence of its towering figures returned right into the room.

Greaves, the visionary behind Symbiopsychotaxiplasm: Take One (1968), left behind 60,000 feet of 16mm footage to be rediscovered for this film. His son David Greaves (one of the original camera operators) and David’s daughter Liani bring the footage into the present as both family inheritance and public archive. Premiering at Sundance before screening in Cannes Directors’ Fortnight, the film is a portal into a room of style, memory, disagreement, and brilliance that reminds us a renaissance is not only remembered, it is reborn.

It’s both a sublime hang-out of a film and a celebration of individual achievements, a fascinating map of a long-ago scene and a referendum on legacy. That this sumptuous footage, allowed room to breathe, exists at all feels like a miracle; that it takes shape here as a coherent, inventive yet straightforwardly informative film is an intergenerational feat… a faultless, captivating experience.

Juan José Campanella’s adaptation of Eduardo Sacheri’s novel winds back through the past to unravel a brutal crime, in the process taking a good, hard look at the legal system.

Campanella (who also wrote the screenplay) frames the story in flashbacks, as a retired government lawyer reworks a book about a case that still bothers him, 25 years after the rape and murder of a beautiful young bride. Benjamin (Ricardo Darin) takes his manuscript to Irene (Soledad Villamil), who is now a judge, but who was his boss back then. She is reluctant to revisit those days for reasons both personal and political…

At first the case is closed too soon by a judge more mindful of crime stats than justice, while the key suspect hovers just beyond reach. It is the commitment of the victim’s widower that inspires Benjamin, when he happens to bump into him a year later, staking out a commuter station as he says he does every morning, waiting and praying for the time when the murderer crosses his path. The young lawyer is struck not just by this man’s anger, but by his devotion to the memory of his wife. He wonders if the system doesn’t owe him more, and in convincing Irene that it does he opens her eyes to his own unspoken ardor.

Campanella lays it out carefully and patiently, and the performances are so good, and the writing is strong enough, that the movie commands our attention. It draws you in and envelopes you in the dynamics of the characters.

“What am I working on? Sure, he wants to get science reporter Geena Davis in the sack, but he means it too. Not that David Cronenberg shows much interest in teleportation — Brundle’s hokey (but spectacular!) invention. Nor does he hang his scientist for Frankensteinian hubris. Rather, this is a film about fusion. Fusion between man and insect, of course; but also the emotional and physical fusion that can occur between man and woman, liberating and painful as that may be.

The playful, quirky chemistry established between Goldblum and Davis (they married soon after) ensures that this gothic horror is heartbreaking as well as stomach churning, though the special effects by Chris Walas remain staggering even today. It may not be the most respectable movie from the man most consider Canada’s greatest filmmaker, but this is surely the most moving.

How does a filmmaker get the greenlight for their dream documentary project amid an ongoing industry contraction? If you’re the idiosyncratic mastermind behind HBO’s How To with John Wilson, you attend a workshop on pitching saccharine Hallmark movies then apply all the same best practices to your own film: an in-depth investigation of concrete (the most ubiquitous of building materials).

With his first feature, documentarian and humourist Wilson continues his methodology of starting with a seemingly straighforward idea and using it as a jumping off point for frequently absurd and endlessly entertaining detours, asides, and digressions. Consistently laugh-out-loud funny, compelling and surprising.

Book Now More Info
moreInfo:
“If you don’t have graft, you’d have a low type of person in politics. Men with no ambition.”

Dan McGinty’s record-breaking efforts at repeat voting (at $2 a pop) commend him to big city boss Akim Tamiroff, who runs “The Machine,” a term that would have been familiar to everyone back in 1940 and which might be due a comeback. Eventually installed as state governor, complete with a pre-selected bride (his secretary), McGinty makes the mistake of falling in love with his honest wife. Her virtue will be his ruination.

Related in flashback, Preston Sturges’ classic is an omnivorous satire on corruption and marked his intentions to bring dramatic realism into American comedy. Sturges was a well-established screenwriter by the late 30s and — perhaps inspired by Orson Welles’ deal at RKO — sold this script for $10 in return for the privilege of directing it himself. (Billy Wilder and John Huston would follow suit soon afterwards.) Over the next 12 months he would write and direct three more, including the indelible The Lady Eve and Sullivan’s Travels, a significant influence on the Coen Brothers’s Barton Fink. Still, the purpose of today’s screening is to remind us that electoral corruption goes back a long ways.

Capra with the gloves off.

Raymond Durgnat

Ladies and gentlemen and registered voters of this fair metropolis, here is a picture which really captures the rowdy spirit of corrupt politics, which makes titanic sport of the brazen peculations of grafting opportunists and which reflects by innuendo the indifference of the American “sucker” […] There was a time—and that not so long ago—when such good-natured elbow-rubbing, even upon the screen, with crooked political bosses, ward-heelers and profligate officios might not have been so amusing for the local constituents. Bosley Crowther, New York Times

The story of an unmade screenplay from the writer of Citizen Kane. In 1932, Herman Mankiewicz wrote a film that foretold the persecution of the Jews and the war in Europe. But Hollywood wouldn't take the risk and The Mad Dog of Europe was never made.
Book Now More Info
moreInfo:
In 1932 (a year before Adolph Hitler became Chancellor of Germany) Herman J Mankiewicz wrote an original screenplay, The Mad Dog of Europe, a film that reflected the rise of “Adolph Mitler” and anticipated the Nazis’ persecution of the Jews, the events of Kristallnacht (that would play out in 1938), and the war that was to consume Europe by the end of the decade.

Mankiewicz — who would go on to write Citizen Kane with Orson Welles — recognized just how dangerous Hitler was, and wanted to use the film to mobilize public opinion against him. But even though the major Hollywood studios were run by Jews, no one was willing to back the project. Anti-Semitism was rife in America, this topic was too hot to handle. Even the anti-defamation league opposed the production. So too did Germany’s consul to Los Angeles, who exerted considerable influence behind the scenes. This is the story of one of the important movies never made.

For more of Hollywood’s response to the rise of nazism, see The Mortal Storm, Three Comrades, and To Be Or Not To Be at VIFF Centre this week.

Eighty years ago, Allied troops were coming home after the long, bloody but decisive war against fascism. Moved by an article in Time magazine about the difficulties they faced in readjusting to civilian life, producer Sam Goldwyn commissioned a screenplay from playwright Sherwood Anderson.

Directed by William Wyler, the most acclaimed director of the day (he had experienced combat himself making propaganda films during the war), The Best Years of Our Lives is remarkable for its candor and sensitivity around issues like PTSD, disabilities, isolationism, and the nuclear age. The film went on to win seven Academy Awards, including Best Picture, Director, Actor (Frederic March), and Supporting Actor (Harold Russell)… In fact, it also won an 8th statuette, because Russell, who lost his hands in the war, was presented with a special award “for bringing hope and courage to his fellow veterans.” The cinematography, by Gregg Toland (Citizen Kane) should also have been recognized. It remains one of the crowning achievements of the golden age of the studio era.

Surprisingly modern… lean, direct, honest about issues that Hollywood then studiously avoided […] As long as we have wars and returning veterans, some of them wounded, The Best Years of Our Lives will not be dated.

Roger Ebert

William Wyler’s intimate epic, from 1946 profoundly and sensitively balances the private demons of scarred veterans and the press of public policies that leave their mark on daily life. Wyler, working with a script by Robert E. Sherwood, captures the sense of history being written on the fly, of momentous shifts in mind-sets and expectations. In the movie’s nearly three-hour span, the chrysalis of an old world seems to crack open and a fragile new one begins to emerge; a deep and tender romanticism arises from the exposed vulnerabilities.

Film

Chris Marker's dazzling and discursive essay film ranges across Japan, Africa, San Francisco, Iceland, politics, philosophy, ritual, movies and memory. It's a film for the permanently curious.
Book Now More Info
moreInfo:
Filmed with a silent 16mm camera and a rudimentary tape recorder, Chris Marker’s essay film could be described as the most dazzling home movie you’ll ever see. Not that Marker — a Frenchman who rubbed shoulders with the nouvelle vague — spends much time at home. There’s footage here he shot in Iceland (supposedly for a planned sci-fi film), Japan, Guinea-Bissau, Cape Verde and San Francisco. Incorporating movie clips and early digital post-production effects, Marker — using the alias Sandor Krasna — ruminates on topics that range freely from ritual, philosophy, politics, movies and memory. It’s a work of great erudition but also poetic and playful, a movie for the permanently curious, a movie about connection, the creation of meaning, souvenirs for the mind.

Sunday’s Pantheon screening will feature a 15-minute introduction by a local film scholar and be followed by an audience talkback.

For anyone who has not seen a Chris Marker film, their varied effects may be compared with that in reading the journal of some eighteenth century traveler: Johnson in the Hebrides, Rousseau’s promenade through his own sensibility, or Goethe’s visit to Rome. The work is based on the assumption that a cultivated man should express himself in words or in film. Add to that the engaging fusion of seriousness and humour; a precise eye for strange places and a quizzical response to unfamiliar people… Beneath all this, there is the unaffected independence of a man who sees that all people are travelers, lonely or self-sufficient, whether they lap the earth or stay at home.

David Thomson, A Biographical Dictionary of Film

The consummate cine-essay, framed as reportage from a roving cineaste, built mainly from Marker’s observations of the ’empire of signs’ that is modern Japan and the poverty endemic in Guinea Bissau. Entertainingly provocative speculations on the ’post-political’ world, haunted by the piano music of Mussorgsky.

Tony Rayns, Sight & Sound

A reverie on Japan, technology, and the conjunction of different times and peoples in the world. It shows how rich the potential is for filmmaking, like the writing of essays and the keeping of journals.

David Thomson

I Am Not a Witch

Film

Rungano Nyoni's acclaimed debut feature is a visually striking satire about a 9-year-old orphan accused of witchcraft in contemporary Zambia. Screening in the latest African Cinema Now! series, The Witch at the Edge of the Screen.
Book Now More Info
moreInfo:
The latest iteration of Akojo Film Collective’s recurring African Cinema Now! series is titled The Witch at the Edge of the Screen and platforms movies in which African women, often vilified and persecuted, turn the tables on their oppressors.

Rungano Nyoni crafts a satiric feminist fairy-tale set in present-day Zambia. When 9-year old orphan Shula is accused of witchcraft, she is exiled to a witch camp run by Mr. Banda, a corrupt and inept government official. Tied to the ground by a white ribbon, Shula is told that she will turn into a goat if she tries to escape. As the only child witch, Shula quickly becomes a local star and the adults around her exploit her supposed powers for financial gain. Soon she is forced to make a difficult decision – whether to resign herself to life in the camp, or take a risk for freedom.

Curatorial note: “Nyoni’s feminist satire takes on the location of the witch camp as a site of disenfranchisement through the often comedic yet harrowing experiences faced by a child accused of witchcraft. When the community turns against her and she is cast into a camp of witches, we are able to follow a deep line of inquiry that opens up the world of witch accusations and the weight and mark it leaves on the lives of women affected.” Akojo Film Collective

Possibly the year’s most audacious film debut, I Am Not A Witch has won numerous awards, including Britain’s BAFTA for best first feature, and to see it is to understand why… Written and directed by Zambian-born, Wales-raised Rungano Nyoni, this smart and savage satire is impressive for the way it joins a dramatically involving story with a Swiftian tale of human society in general and Africa culture and customs in particular… Beguiling… wickedly smart.

Kenneth Turan, Los Angeles Times

For all its factual grounding, I Am Not a Witch is also a work of fairytale invention, unravelling the threads of its quasi-mythical narrative with anarchic aplomb… Margaret Mulubwa is a mesmerising screen presence, her stoical countenance broken occasionally by a radiant smile that lights up the landscape.

Peter Bradshaw, The Guardian

Beautiful and unsettling…It is a remarkable, strange and politically potent first film.

Michael O’Sullivan, The Washington Post

“Anyone you walk past on the pavement anywhere might be a sadist, a compulsive thief or even a murderer,” Patricia Highsmith wrote to a friend. “I can think of nothing more apt to set the imagination stirring.” It’s the sort of sentiment that Alfred Hitchcock would surely endorse, and so perhaps it’s no surprise that Highsmith’s first novel, written in 1948, should have been snapped up by the movies’ “master of suspense”, and became one of his most enduring, popular films.

The idea is simple and fiendish. Sociopath Charles Bruno (played with silky insouciance by Robert Walker) strikes up a conversation with star tennis player Guy Haynes (Farley Granger) and makes him a gentleman’s proposition: Bruno will do Guy the kindness of getting rid of his unloved wife, on the understanding that he will return the favour. “Criss-cross.” Guy is appalled, of course. But not entirely innocent, either. Highsmith and Hitchcock both knew or suspected that in certain circumstances, any one of us might be capable of almost anything…

Another great crime writer, Raymond Chandler, cowrote the screenplay. And this abundantly entertaining movie ushered in what would be a golden era for Hitchcock, the decade that would produce Rear Window, Vertigo, North by Northwest, The Wrong Man among others.

I know no other recent film, in fact, which better conveys the condition of modern man, who must escape his fate without the help of the gods.

Jean-Luc Godard, Cahiers du Cinema

This singular Senegalese melodrama charts the struggles of orphaned teenage twins Awa and her brother Adama. The latter dreams of a new life in Europe while Adama has to cope with the unwanted attentions of her uncle. Director Moussa Sene Absa keeps us on our toes switching between different time lines and throwing in commentary from a griot and a women’s choir.

Curatorial note: “Awa grows up in a tight family unit under the lyrical eyes of a chorus that reaches into the stories and lives of the community and the people intertwined within it. When a disaster alters her future, the community and its structures that enable gender based violence come into focus. Not only must she reckon with the new future that unfolds; she must also attend to the ghost of her past and the man who causes this rupture.” Akojo Film Collective

The latest film from the veteran Senegalese director blends narrative styles and traditions with abandon, running the gamut from local folklore to Western-style soap opera… it’s consistently, colorfully diverting and honestly felt, likely to enchant many a curious art house patron who stumbles upon it.

Guy Lodge, Variety

Wrapping up our current FRAMEWORK series, film scholar Michael van den Bos introduces Hitchcock’s most underrated film, The Wrong Man.

Based on an actual case of a New York musician who was identified as a violent criminal and whose protestations of innocence were never believed, this is the film where Hitchcock’s preoccupation with the fate of an innocent man in the wrong place at the wrong time gets its most severe and soul-searching treatment. It is the odd one out among Hitchcock movies of the 50s: black and white, stripped of glamour and not at all interested in showing us a good time. Yet is one of his greatest accomplishments, a Kafkaesque, expressionist masterpiece, and for all its restraint, one of his most moving films.

Truffaut: “Hitchcock has never been more himself than in this film, which nevertheless runs the risk of disappointing lovers of suspense and English humour. There is very little suspense in it and almost no humour, English or otherwise. The Wrong Man is Hitchcock’s most stripped down film since Lifeboat; it is the roast without the gravy, the news event served up raw and, as Bresson would say, ’without adornment.’ […] Hitchcock offers a film about the role of the accused man, an accused man and the fragility of human testimony and justice. It has nothing in common with documentaries except in appearance; in its pessimism and skepticism I believe it is closer to Night and Fog… In any case, it is perhaps his best film, the one that goes farthest in the direction he chose so long ago.” (1957)

A woefully underrated and truly harrowing study of the psychological cost of misguided suspicion and mistaken identity.

Eric Henderson, Slant

Perhaps his best film.

Francois Truffaut

moreInfo:
A year comes in and a year goes out… Vincente Minnelli’s heartwarming evergreen chronicles an ordinarily tumultuous year in the life of a prosperous household in 1904, when the worst prospect that faces them is a potential move to New York City. It’s frightening because it means change, and that’s inevitable – but it doesn’t mean we shouldn’t cherish what we share now, our past together. It’s debatable that MGM ever conjured a more affecting musical, and producer Arthur Freed, who headed their musical department, considered this one his personal favourite.

Tunes include The Trolley Song, The Boy Next Door, and Have Yourself a Merry Little Christmas.

Sunday’s Pantheon screening will feature a 15-minute introduction by a local film scholar and be followed by an audience talkback.

An unmissable big-screen experience.

Peter Bradshaw, The Guardian

A movie that defines perfection, as it captures the spirit of hope and anxiety that informed the last years of the second world war, when it was made. It’s a film whose four parts cover the seasons from summer to spring but is truly a film for all seasons and all time.

Philip French, The Observer

Minnelli’s captivating musical still comes up fresh as paint with each successive viewing.

Tom Milne, Time Out
